mcqs.q: The 'aspiration pathway' of the oral-lung axis refers to:
opts: Inhaling oral bacteria (from plaque) into the lower respiratory tract
Cytokines travelling from gums to lungs
mcqs.explain: The aspiration pathway is the inhalation of oral bacteria from plaque/infected gums directly into the lower airway, contributing to lung infection.

mcqs.q: COPD is most commonly caused by:
mcqs.explain: Smoking is the leading cause of COPD, though passive smoke, fumes and pollution also contribute.

mcqs.q: Chronic bronchitis is clinically defined as a productive cough for:
opts: At least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years
mcqs.explain: Chronic bronchitis is defined by a chronic productive cough for at least three months a year over two consecutive years; emphysema is alveolar destruction.

mcqs.q: Why must high-flow oxygen be AVOIDED in advanced COPD?
opts: These patients rely on a hypoxic drive — high O₂ can cause respiratory arrest (limit to 2–3 L/min)
Oxygen is toxic to the teeth
mcqs.explain: In advanced COPD the respiratory drive depends on low oxygen, so high-flow O₂ can cause respiratory arrest; supplemental O₂ is limited to 2–3 L/min.

mcqs.q: Nitrous oxide is avoided in COPD because it:
opts: Can accumulate in lung bullae and cause a pneumothorax
mcqs.explain: Nitrous oxide can diffuse into and expand enlarged air spaces (bullae) in the COPD lung, risking a pneumothorax.

mcqs.q: Because of orthopnea, a COPD patient should be treated:
mcqs.explain: Reclining causes a 'drowning' sensation (abdominal contents press on the diaphragm), so COPD patients are treated semi-upright.

mcqs.q: Asthma is best described as:
opts: Chronic airway inflammation with reversible airflow obstruction
mcqs.explain: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation causing variable, reversible expiratory airflow limitation — wheeze, breathlessness and cough.

mcqs.q: About 5–10% of severe asthmatics react to local anaesthetic with epinephrine because of the:
opts: Metabisulfite preservative — use a plain anaesthetic (3% mepivacaine)
mcqs.explain: Metabisulfite, the antioxidant preservative in vasoconstrictor-containing LA, can trigger an attack in sulfite-sensitive asthmatics — use plain mepivacaine.

mcqs.q: Which analgesics should be AVOIDED in an asthmatic patient?
opts: Aspirin and NSAIDs (can trigger an 'aspirin-induced' attack)
mcqs.explain: Aspirin/NSAIDs shift arachidonic acid metabolism toward leukotrienes, which can trigger a severe aspirin-induced asthma attack.

mcqs.q: For sedation in an asthmatic, which drugs are AVOIDED due to histamine release/bronchospasm?
mcqs.explain: Narcotics and barbiturates release histamine and can cause bronchospasm; hydroxyzine and benzodiazepines are preferred.

mcqs.q: Which finding indicates acute SEVERE asthma during a dental procedure?
opts: Inability to complete a sentence, RR ≥30, O₂ sat <90%
A calm patient with normal speech
mcqs.explain: Acute severe asthma: inability to complete a sentence in one breath, RR ≥30/min, tachycardia ≥120/min and O₂ saturation <90%.

mcqs.q: The immediate management of an acute asthma attack in the chair is:
opts: Stop, give a β₂-agonist inhaler and oxygen; epinephrine SC if worsening
Lay the patient flat and continue
mcqs.explain: Discontinue, position comfortably, give a β₂-agonist inhaler/nebuliser and oxygen (6 L); if no improvement, give subcutaneous epinephrine and call for help.

mcqs.q: Chronic use of inhaled corticosteroids predisposes asthmatics to which oral problem?
opts: Oral candidiasis (thrush) — advise rinsing after use
mcqs.explain: Inhaled corticosteroids alter the oral flora and increase candidiasis risk; patients should rinse the mouth after inhaler use.

mcqs.q: Regular professional dental cleaning reduces the recurrence of pneumonia in older adults by nearly:
mcqs.explain: Professional cleaning lowers oral bacterial load and reduces pneumonia recurrence by nearly 50%, especially in older adults.

mcqs.q: Tuberculosis is caused by:
opts: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by airborne droplets
mcqs.explain: TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transmitted person-to-person via airborne droplets from coughs and sneezes.

mcqs.q: The difference between latent and active TB is that latent TB:
opts: Is inactive and symptomless (standard precautions); active TB is infectious
mcqs.explain: Latent TB is inactive and symptomless (patients can be treated with standard precautions); active TB multiplies, causes illness and is infectious.

mcqs.q: A patient with ACTIVE pulmonary TB needing routine dental care should be:
opts: Postponed until non-infectious (≈2–3 weeks therapy + negative sputum)
Treated immediately in the open clinic
Given a standard surgical mask and treated
mcqs.explain: Active TB patients should not receive routine care; defer until non-infectious — usually after 2–3 weeks of therapy with negative sputum smears (×3).

mcqs.q: To protect against TB transmission, dental personnel should wear:
opts: N95/FFP3 respirators (standard surgical masks are inadequate)
mcqs.explain: Standard surgical masks do not protect against TB; specialized N95/FFP3 respirators are required, and emergency care needs a negative-pressure room.

mcqs.q: Oral tuberculosis lesions typically appear as:
opts: Painful, chronic, irregular ulcers (often on the tongue or gingiva)
Painless white patches that rub off
mcqs.explain: Oral TB often presents as painful, chronic, irregular ulcers on the tongue or gingiva — include them in the differential of a suspicious ulcer.

mcqs.q: The anti-TB drug rifampicin can cause which side effects relevant to dentistry?
mcqs.explain: Rifampicin can cause thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity and increased cortisol metabolism.

mcqs.q: Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by:
opts: Throat muscles relaxing and blocking the airway during sleep
A blood clot in the lung
mcqs.explain: OSA is the repeated stopping of breathing as the throat muscles relax and block the airway; dentists are often first to spot it.

mcqs.q: Which dental sign is a classic 'red flag' for obstructive sleep apnea?
opts: Bruxism (tooth grinding) with worn, flattened teeth
mcqs.explain: When the airway collapses, the jaw subconsciously clenches; bruxism with worn/chipped teeth is a key OSA red flag, along with dry mouth and a scalloped tongue.

mcqs.q: A 'scalloped tongue' in a patient with suspected OSA suggests:
opts: A tongue too large for the mouth pressing against the teeth
mcqs.explain: A large tongue (a common physical cause of OSA) presses against the teeth, creating ridges/a scalloped appearance along the edges.

mcqs.q: Which oral appliance does a dentist provide for mild-to-moderate OSA?
opts: A night guard that closes the airway
mcqs.explain: Dentists fabricate mandibular advancement devices (which move the lower jaw forward) or tongue-retaining devices for mild-to-moderate OSA.

mcqs.q: Before treating any asthmatic patient, you should ensure:
opts: Their rescue inhaler (albuterol) is available on the bracket table
mcqs.explain: Have the patient's reliever inhaler (albuterol) on the bracket table, treat only well-controlled asthma, and keep oxygen and epinephrine ready.

mcqs.q: To screen for OSA, dentists may use:
opts: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale and refer for polysomnography
mcqs.explain: Dentists screen with questionnaires like the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and oral exams, then refer for a formal sleep study (polysomnography).

mcqs.q: Why is periodontitis relevant in COPD?
opts: It shares risk factors and can promote COPD progression via microbial/immune imbalance
It has no link to the lungs
mcqs.explain: Periodontitis and COPD share risk factors (e.g. smoking); periodontitis can promote COPD progression through microbial and immune imbalance.

saqs.q: Describe the three pathways of the oral-lung axis.
saqs.a: Aspiration (inhaling oral bacteria into the lower airway), inflammatory (gum cytokines like IL-6 reaching the lungs), and medicative (lung drugs/inhalers causing oral disease).

saqs.q: List the dental precautions in COPD.
saqs.a: Limit O₂ to 2–3 L/min (hypoxic drive — high O₂ → respiratory arrest); avoid nitrous oxide (bullae → pneumothorax); treat semi-upright (orthopnea); short morning visits; cautious rubber dam.

saqs.q: Summarise the drug cautions in asthma.
saqs.a: Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs (leukotriene/aspirin-induced attack); use plain anaesthetic (3% mepivacaine) in sulfite-sensitive patients; avoid narcotics/barbiturates (bronchospasm); inhaled steroids → candidiasis.

saqs.q: Recognise and manage acute severe asthma in the dental chair.
saqs.a: Recognise: can't complete a sentence, RR ≥30, tachycardia ≥120, O₂ sat <90%. Manage: stop, position comfortably, β₂-agonist inhaler + oxygen (6 L); if worsening, subcutaneous epinephrine and call for help.

saqs.q: Contrast latent and active TB and give the infection-control rules.
saqs.a: Latent: inactive, symptomless, standard precautions. Active: infectious — defer routine care until non-infectious (≈2–3 weeks + negative sputum). Use N95/FFP3 masks (not surgical) and a negative-pressure room for emergencies.

saqs.q: List the oral manifestations and drug effects of TB.
saqs.a: Oral: painful chronic irregular ulcers (tongue/gingiva). Anti-TB drugs (rifampicin) → thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, increased cortisol metabolism. Screen for chronic cough/fever/weight loss.

saqs.q: Describe the dentist's role in obstructive sleep apnea.
saqs.a: Spot oral signs (bruxism, dry mouth, scalloped tongue, TMJ pain), screen (Epworth scale) and refer for polysomnography, and provide oral appliances (mandibular advancement devices) for mild-to-moderate OSA.
